title: Cook without power
keywords: light gas burner with a match
summary: Never cook with a grill, camp stove or charcoal indoors, and never heat the house with a gas oven or range. Indoors, cook on a fireplace or wood stove vented to the outside and set up for cooking, or on a gas range’s surface burners lit by match only if your model’s manual allows it, watched the whole time. Otherwise cook outdoors, at least 20 feet (6 m) from windows, or eat food cold. Cook meat, poultry, eggs and leftovers to the temperatures in the table, checked with a food thermometer.
doFirst: Never burn charcoal, or use a grill, hibachi, fuel lantern or camp stove indoors, and never heat the house with a gas oven or range (CDC, CPSC).
Never run a generator in the house, garage, basement, crawlspace, shed, porch or carport, even with doors and windows open (CDC, CPSC). See Generators.
Indoors, cook on a fireplace or wood stove that is vented to the outside, set up for cooking, and has a vent that needs no power to work (EPA), under every rule in Wood stoves and fireplaces.

Gas or propane range: surface burners only, lit by match only if your model’s manual says it can be, watched the whole time, never to heat the room (GE, Whirlpool, KitchenAid, Wolf). No manual to hand, or it says no: don’t.
Otherwise cook outdoors, at least 20 feet (6 m) from windows (Ready.gov), or eat food cold. Store-bought canned food can be eaten from the can without warming (Ready.gov).

blocks.warn: Never heat the house with a gas oven or range (CDC, CPSC). CDC: “Don’t cook or burn anything on a stove or fireplace that isn’t vented.”

list: Never burn charcoal, or use a grill, hibachi, fuel lantern or camp stove indoors (CDC, CPSC). Charcoal grills and camp stoves are for outdoor use only (Ready.gov).
Never use a grill in a garage, breezeway, carport or porch, next to the house, or under anything that can burn (New York State Division of Consumer Protection).
Never run a generator in the house, garage, basement, crawlspace, shed, porch or carport, even with doors and windows open (CDC, CPSC).
Don’t bring a grill inside with coals that were just used: charcoal gives off carbon monoxide until it is completely out (New York State Division of Consumer Protection).

blocks.label: Carbon monoxide and burning fuel indoors

blocks.p: EPA: during a power outage, you can cook indoors on a vented fireplace or a vented wood stove, if it is set up for cooking. A vented appliance can be used to cook indoors only if its vent does not need power to work (EPA). Ready.gov also lists a fireplace for cooking in an emergency.

list: Only a fireplace or wood stove vented to the outside (CDC, EPA). Every rule in Wood stoves and fireplaces applies, among them: “Open the damper before you light a fire, and never close it until the fire is out and the embers are cold (Massachusetts Department of Fire Services).” “Keep anything that can burn at least 3 feet (1 m) from the fireplace or stove (US Fire Administration).” “Put the fire out before you go to sleep or leave the house (US Fire Administration, FEMA).”
Never use charcoal in a fireplace: it can cause carbon monoxide poisoning (EPA).

Make sure the house has carbon monoxide alarms (EPA). Wood stoves and fireplaces: “Put a smoke alarm and a battery-operated carbon monoxide alarm near the area you heat, and test them every month (CDC).”
A vent-free gas fireplace or gas logs are not vented. Don’t cook on them (CDC: “Don’t cook or burn anything on a stove or fireplace that isn’t vented.”).

blocks.p: The range makers GE, Whirlpool, KitchenAid and Wolf say the surface burners of a gas range can be lit by hand with a match in a power outage, on models that allow it. No government agency page opened for this app says anything about cooking on a range in an outage. EPA’s outage guidance names only “a vented fireplace or a vented wood stove or another vented fuel burning stove, if it is set up for cooking”, and says “Unvented combustion appliances should not be used to cook indoors, or for any other indoor use.”

blocks.warn: Never heat the house with a gas oven or range (CDC, CPSC).

list: Check your model’s manual first. Light a burner by hand only if the manual says your model can be lit that way: some models have a safety feature that prevents it (Whirlpool, KitchenAid). No manual to hand, or it doesn’t allow it: the answer is no, and you cook outdoors or eat food cold.

Surface burners only. Never the oven: it can’t be lit by hand in an outage (GE, Whirlpool, KitchenAid). Never a griddle, grill, French top or charbroiler on the range (Wolf; Whirlpool: the vent may not be working).
Light it the way your manual says. The makers’ steps: hold a lit long match or lighter at the burner first, then turn the knob (GE, KitchenAid; Wolf: an ignitor at least 6 inches (15 cm) long).
A burner is either lit or off. With no power there is no automatic relight (Wolf). If the flame goes out, gas keeps flowing: turn the knob to Off (GE).
Watch the burner the whole time it is lit (Wolf: monitor the gas burner closely).
Never use it to heat the room (Wolf: do not use surface burners to heat the kitchen).

blocks.p: Carbon monoxide alarms, and what to do when one sounds, are in Carbon monoxide and burning fuel indoors.

blocks.label: Carbon monoxide and burning fuel indoors

sections.h: Burners that are not on the list

blocks.p: Ready.gov also lists candle warmers, chafing dishes and fondue pots for cooking in an emergency. They burn fuel in the room, and no source opened for this app says how to use them indoors without carbon monoxide building up. This app’s own caution: don’t use them while the power is out.
While you shelter from fallout, cook only on what Living in a closed-up house allows: warmth without flame comes first there, and going outdoors to cook is a trip outside.

list: Use grills and camp stoves outside only, in a well-ventilated area (Ready.gov, New York State Division of Consumer Protection).

Keep grills and camp stoves at least 20 feet (6 m) from windows (Ready.gov), a safe distance from the house’s doors and any air intakes for its heating or cooling system (EPA), and at least 10 feet (3 m) from the side of any building unless the grill maker’s instructions say it can be closer (Massachusetts Department of Fire Services).
Not under overhanging branches, and away from deck railings (Massachusetts Department of Fire Services).
Never leave a burning grill unattended (Massachusetts Department of Fire Services).
Keep children and pets 3 feet (1 m) away from grills (Massachusetts Department of Fire Services).

Charcoal: use only charcoal starter fluid, and never add lighter fluid to burning briquettes or hot coals (Massachusetts Department of Fire Services). New York’s Division of Consumer Protection suggests lighting charcoal in a charcoal chimney, with no lighter fluid at all.

Ashes: let the coals burn out completely, then cool for 48 hours before you get rid of them. If you must get rid of them sooner, soak them thoroughly in water and put them in a metal container (Massachusetts Department of Fire Services).
Propane grill: if you smell gas while cooking, turn the grill off and get away from it. Never use a match or lighter to look for a leak (Massachusetts Department of Fire Services).

blocks.p: Cooking over an open fire: build and put out the fire as in Fire. Fuel and propane cylinders: see Store fuel safely and Kerosene and propane heaters.

The only way to tell if food is cooked enough to kill germs is a food thermometer. You can’t tell by its color and texture (CDC). Cook food to these temperatures before you take it off the heat, measured with a food thermometer (USDA).

head: Food
Cook to at least
rows: Beef, pork, veal and lamb steaks, chops and roasts (not wild game)
Ham, fresh or smoked (uncooked; not wild boar)
All poultry: breasts, whole bird, legs, thighs, wings, ground poultry, giblets and stuffing
All wild game and wild birds, in the thickest part

blocks.p: Table from USDA; CDC gives the same. The wild game row is Field dressing game’s rule: “Cook all wild game and birds to at least 165°F in the thickest part, and fish to 145°F.” And: “Bear and wild boar can carry trichinella worms. Cook them to 165°F.” Wild game, ground or whole, is always 165°F (73.9°C).

list: Not eating it straight away? Keep cooked food hot, at 140°F (60°C) or above (FoodSafety.gov).
Leftovers and anything left out: how long they can wait is in Is it still good?
Store-bought canned food can be eaten from the can without warming (Ready.gov).
Keep food on hand that needs no refrigeration and can be eaten cold (USDA).

blocks.p: Water for drinking, cooking and washing must be bottled, boiled or treated (CDC). How to boil or treat it is in Make water safe.
